The inflammatory response to tu- berculosis can cause considerable tissue damage and ad- junctive steroid therapy may be used to counter this. Cor- ticosteroids are of little benefit in uncomplicated pulmonary tuberculosis. However, a study25 found adjunc- tive dexamethasone improved survival, but probably not severe disability, in adolescents and adults with tubercu- lous meningitis. Systematic reviews of tuberculous pleurisy26 and pericarditis,27 have concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of corticosteroids in these conditions. WHO17 suggests that corticosteroids may be useful adjuvants to antituberculous therapy for the management of tuberculous meningitis, pericarditis, pleu- ral effusion, laryngitis, tuberculosis of the renal tract, adrenocortical insufficiency due to adrenal gland tubercu- losis, and massive lymph node enlargement in both HIV- positive and -negative patients. Corticosteroids may also be useful for hypersensitivity reactions to antituberculosis drugs. For further details on the possible role of cortico- steroids as an adjunct to antituberculous therapy, see p.1514. Studies have suggested that injection of suspensions of killed Mycobacterium vaccae improved immune respon- siveness in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis, although a systematic review28 concluded that M. vaccae immuno- therapy was of no benefit. • Prevention. Studies have found that BCG vaccine offers protection against serious forms of tuberculosis in chil- dren, such as miliary and meningeal tuberculosis, but has variable efficacy against pulmonary tuberculosis in adults. In high prevalence areas, vaccination is recommended for children at birth, except for children with HIV infection. For further information on BCG vaccine see, p.2205. Tuberculosis skin testing may identify persons with latent M. tuberculosis infection. Treatment of tuberculosis skin test-positive persons (also referred to as preventative ther- apy or chemoprophylaxis) reduces the risk of developing (reactivation) tuberculosis. Treatment is beneficial in HIV- infected patients, contacts of active cases, persons who have recently become tuberculosis skin test positive, and persons at high risk of disease. Chemoprophylaxis is not recommended routinely in developing countries where the priority is to detect and treat patients with active tubercu- 198 Antibacterials losis.17,29 Latent tuberculosis has been treated with isoni- azid or rifampicin given alone, or with rifampicin given with either isoniazid or pyrazinamide.
